problems.html: ∫x e2x  dx\displaystyle\int x\,\mathrm{e}^{2x}\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫xe2xdx.
hints: Integration by parts trades one integral for another: ∫u dv=uv−∫v du\int u\,\mathrm{d}v=uv-\int v\,\mathrm{d}u∫udv=uv−∫vdu, so choose uuu to be the part that gets simpler when differentiated.
Take u=xu=xu=x and dv=e2xdx\mathrm{d}v=\mathrm{e}^{2x}\mathrm{d}xdv=e2xdx; then du=dx\mathrm{d}u=\mathrm{d}xdu=dx and the remaining integral has no xxx in it at all.
Do not forget the 12\tfrac1221​ each time you integrate e2x\mathrm{e}^{2x}e2x — it appears twice, once in vvv and once in the final integral.

problems.html: ∫xcos⁡x  dx\displaystyle\int x\cos x\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫xcosxdx.
hints: Choose u=xu=xu=x, so that differentiating it removes the polynomial factor entirely.
Then dv=cos⁡x dx\mathrm{d}v=\cos x\,\mathrm{d}xdv=cosxdx gives v=sin⁡xv=\sin xv=sinx, and the leftover integral is ∫sin⁡x dx\int\sin x\,\mathrm{d}x∫sinxdx.
Watch the sign: ∫sin⁡x dx=−cos⁡x\int\sin x\,\mathrm{d}x=-\cos x∫sinxdx=−cosx, and it enters with a minus in front from the parts formula, so the two minus signs combine.
problems.format: the antiderivative at x = 0, with C = 0

problems.html: ∫xln⁡x  dx\displaystyle\int x\ln x\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫xlnxdx.
hints: Here the usual choice is reversed: take u=ln⁡xu=\ln xu=lnx, because differentiating a logarithm simplifies it while integrating one does not.
So dv=x dx\mathrm{d}v=x\,\mathrm{d}xdv=xdx gives v=12x2v=\tfrac12x^2v=21​x2, and du=dxx\mathrm{d}u=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{x}du=xdx​.
The remaining integral is ∫12x dx\int\tfrac12 x\,\mathrm{d}x∫21​xdx — the xxx in the denominator cancels one power, which is the whole point of the choice.

problems.html: ∫ dx(x−1)(x+1)\displaystyle\int\frac{\,\mathrm{d}x}{(x-1)(x+1)}∫(x−1)(x+1)dx​.
hints: The denominator is already factorised, so split the fraction as Ax−1+Bx+1\dfrac{A}{x-1}+\dfrac{B}{x+1}x−1A​+x+1B​.
Multiply through by (x−1)(x+1)(x-1)(x+1)(x−1)(x+1) and substitute the two convenient values x=1x=1x=1 and x=−1x=-1x=−1 to pick off AAA and BBB one at a time.
Each piece then integrates to a logarithm; combining them with the log laws gives a single logarithm of a quotient.
problems.format: the antiderivative at x = 3 (C = 0), to 3 d.p.

problems.html: ∫3x+1x(x+1)  dx\displaystyle\int\frac{3x+1}{x(x+1)}\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫x(x+1)3x+1​dx.
hints: Split into Ax+Bx+1\dfrac{A}{x}+\dfrac{B}{x+1}xA​+x+1B​ and clear the denominators.
Substituting x=0x=0x=0 gives AAA immediately, and x=−1x=-1x=−1 gives BBB.
Both pieces integrate to logarithms; keep the modulus signs, since the arguments change sign across the excluded points.
problems.format: the antiderivative at x = 1 (C = 0), to 3 d.p.

problems.html: ∫sin⁡2x  dx\displaystyle\int\sin^2 x\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫sin2xdx.
hints: An even power of sine cannot be done by substitution — you need to lower the power first.
Use the double-angle identity in the form sin⁡2x=12(1−cos⁡2x)\sin^2x=\tfrac12(1-\cos 2x)sin2x=21​(1−cos2x).
Now integrate term by term, remembering that ∫cos⁡2x dx\int\cos 2x\,\mathrm{d}x∫cos2xdx carries a compensating 12\tfrac1221​.

hints: An odd power of cosine is the easy case: peel off one factor of cos⁡x\cos xcosx to pair with dx\mathrm{d}xdx.
Write cos⁡3x=(1−sin⁡2x)cos⁡x\cos^3x=(1-\sin^2x)\cos xcos3x=(1−sin2x)cosx using the Pythagorean identity.
Now substitute u=sin⁡xu=\sin xu=sinx, so du=cos⁡x dx\mathrm{d}u=\cos x\,\mathrm{d}xdu=cosxdx and the integral becomes a polynomial in uuu.

Use the identity tan⁡2x=sec⁡2x−1\tan^2x=\sec^2x-1tan2x=sec2x−1.

After the first round you are left with ∫2xsin⁡x dx\int 2x\sin x\,\mathrm{d}x∫2xsinxdx — apply parts again to that.

Apply parts once more to that, by the same trick, to finish.

Apply parts twice, keeping the same choice of which factor to differentiate both times, until the original integral reappears on the right.

questions.stem: In ∫x2ln⁡x dx\displaystyle\int x^{2}\ln x\,\mathrm{d}x∫x2lnxdx, which factor should be taken as uuu when integrating by parts?

questions.hint: Ask what each factor becomes when you differentiate it, and which choice leaves you an integral simpler than the one you started with.
questions.why: LIATE ranks Logarithm ahead of Algebraic, and the reason is practical rather than arbitrary. Differentiating ln⁡x\ln xlnx gives 1x\dfrac1xx1​, which cancels a power of the other factor and leaves an elementary integral. Taking u=x2u=x^2u=x2 instead forces you to integrate ln⁡x\ln xlnx first — possible, but it needs its own application of parts and produces a messier integral than the one you started with. The choice does not change the answer, only how much work reaching it costs.

questions.hint: Count the free constants. Can a single one match a general numerator over a squared factor?

With a single term there are too few free constants to match a general numerator, and the equations turn out inconsistent. The two pieces then integrate quite differently — the first to a logarithm, the second to a negative power — which is why the split is worth making. Note also that the numerator over a linear factor is always a constant, never a linear expression.

questions.stem: On an interval where fff is concave up, how does the trapezium rule compare with the true integral?
options: It is exact.
It may do either, depending on the sign of fff.
It overestimates it.
It underestimates it.
questions.hint: Draw a single strip. When the curve bends upwards, where does the straight chord joining the endpoints sit relative to it?
questions.why: On a concave-up arc the chord joining the two endpoints lies above the curve, so every trapezium contains its true strip and the total comes out too large. Concave down reverses the argument and the rule underestimates. The rule is exact only where fff is linear on each strip, chord and curve then coinciding. The sign of fff is irrelevant: the argument is about which way the curve bends, not how high it sits, and shifting fff upwards adds the same rectangle to both the estimate and the truth. Simpson's rule fits a parabola through three points instead of a chord through two, which is why it does so much better — it is exact for cubics.
